items.q: Why base62 for short codes instead of base64?

options.t: Base64's + and / characters need percent-encoding in URLs, which defeats the point of a short link
options.why: Right. Base62 is just 0-9, a-z, A-Z — every character URL-safe with no escaping. Base64 would give slightly shorter codes but ugly escaped ones.

options.t: Base62 compresses better
options.why: Backwards — more symbols per character means base64 packs MORE into each character. The reason to give that up is URL safety, not compression.

options.t: Base64 is patented
options.why: No — base64 is a free, ancient standard used everywhere. The objection is purely that + and / are not URL-safe characters.

options.t: Databases can't index base64 strings
options.why: Databases index any string happily. The problem lives in the URL bar, not the index: + and / must be escaped in URLs.

items.q: How many distinct codes does base62 with 7 characters give you?

options.t: About 3.5 trillion
options.why: 62^7 ≈ 3.5 × 10^12. Even 6 billion links over five years uses under 0.2% of that space — which is why 7 characters is enough forever and wasted IDs are free.

options.t: About 3.5 billion
options.why: That's closer to 62^5 territory. The jump matters: billions would be tight against a 6-billion-link forecast; trillions makes the space a non-issue.

options.t: About 62 million
options.why: Off by five orders of magnitude — that wouldn't last a month at 100M links/month. Each extra character multiplies the space by 62.

options.t: Exactly 7 × 62 = 434
options.why: Positions multiply, they don't add. Seven independent slots of 62 choices each is 62 × 62 × ... seven times = 62^7.

items.q: The estimation phase reveals the shortener's true character. Which is it?

options.t: Write-heavy and large-data
options.why: Both wrong: writes are ~40/sec (a laptop's workload) and five years of links is ~3 TB. Designing for imaginary write volume is the classic junior misread here.

options.t: Read-heavy and small-data
options.why: Yes — roughly 100 reads per write, and all links ever fit on one drive. So you design for read QPS and latency, and you refuse to shard for data size.

options.t: Read-heavy and large-data
options.why: Half right. Reads dominate, but 6B links × 500 bytes ≈ 3 TB — small data. Saying 'storage is a non-problem' out loud is worth real points.

options.t: Balanced read/write with bursty storage growth
options.why: Nothing balanced about 100:1, and storage grows linearly and slowly. The numbers exist precisely to kill vague characterizations like this.

items.q: What's the behavioral difference between a 301 and a 302 redirect?

options.t: 301 is for HTTPS, 302 for HTTP
options.why: Redirect codes have nothing to do with the transport protocol. The distinction is permanence: whether the browser may remember the answer.

options.t: 301 means 'permanent — browsers may cache it and skip you next time'; 302 means 'temporary — ask me again on every click'
options.why: Exactly, and it's the whole trade-off: 301 offloads repeat clicks to browser caches; 302 brings every click back to your servers where it can be counted, expired, or revoked.

options.t: 302 is faster for the user
options.why: Per-click they're identical — one response either way. If anything, 301 makes REPEAT clicks faster by skipping your server entirely; that skipping is exactly what breaks analytics.

options.t: 301 can only redirect within the same domain
options.why: Both redirect anywhere. The only meaningful difference for a shortener is cacheability — permanent vs ask-again.

items.q: Why does the hash-and-truncate strategy (MD5 the URL, keep 7 characters) require a retry loop?

options.t: Truncating to 7 characters shrinks the space enough that different URLs will sometimes produce the same code — a birthday collision — so inserts must detect the clash and re-salt
options.why: Right. Collisions start around a couple of million links (square root of 3.5T) and by 6 billion links roughly 1 insert in 600 clashes. Each clash means re-hash and retry — unbounded write latency.

options.t: MD5 is too slow to run inline
options.why: Hashing is microseconds — speed is not the issue. The issue is that a truncated hash is no longer collision-resistant, so two URLs can share a code.

options.t: Hashes can produce non-base62 characters
options.why: You just re-encode the hash bits into base62 — a formatting step, not a retry. The retry exists for collisions after truncation.

options.t: The database rejects binary keys
options.why: Keys are stored as text either way. The loop exists because truncation makes collisions statistically inevitable at scale.

items.q: What is a Key Generation Service (KGS) in the classic shortener design?

options.t: A service that hashes URLs on demand
options.why: That's the hash strategy, which a KGS exists to avoid. A KGS mints keys ahead of time, unrelated to any URL's content.

options.t: An offline job that pre-generates a pool of unique random codes, which app servers then claim atomically
options.why: Yes. Uniqueness is checked at generation time, off the hot path, so creates never collide. The cost: an extra service, a keys database, and claim bookkeeping to operate.

options.t: The database's auto-increment feature
options.why: Auto-increment is the raw counter approach — sequential and centralized, the two problems a KGS (or leased ranges) is built to escape.

options.t: A DNS service that assigns short domains
options.why: Domains are fixed; a KGS mints the path tokens (the 7-character codes), not hostnames.

items.q: Two users try to claim the custom alias 'my-launch' in the same millisecond. The correct mechanism to ensure exactly one wins is:

options.t: One atomic conditional insert — put-if-not-exists — and let the database referee
options.why: Right. A single atomic write cannot race: the database serializes the two claims and exactly one succeeds. Uniqueness is enforced by an atomic write, never by a read followed by hope.

options.t: Read to check the alias is free, then insert it
options.why: This is check-then-insert — the classic race. Between your read and your write, the other user's insert lands, and now both believe they own it.

options.t: Lock the whole links table during claims
options.why: It works and it's a sledgehammer: aliases are ~a hundred claims/sec sharing a table with every redirect's metadata. A row-level atomic insert gives the same guarantee at zero contention cost.

options.t: Queue all alias claims through one worker
options.why: Serializing through one consumer does prevent the race, but you've built a coordination service to reproduce what a conditional write gives you in one call.

items.q: In 'lazy expiry', when is an expired link actually caught?

options.t: A cron job checks every link hourly
options.why: That's the sweeper — the hygiene half. Lazy expiry is the correctness half: the read path itself checks the timestamp, so expiry works even if the sweeper never runs.

options.t: At read time — the redirect path checks expires_at on every hit and serves 410 Gone if it's past
options.why: Exactly. The check rides along on a row you already fetched, costs nothing, and is the correctness guarantee. Cleanup of dead rows is a separate, best-effort hygiene job.

options.t: The database refuses to store rows past their expiry
options.why: Databases store whatever you write; TTL features DELETE rows later (best-effort, possibly days late in DynamoDB's case). Something must still answer correctly in the gap — that's the lazy check.

options.t: The browser's cache expires the link
options.why: With our 302 + no-cache choice the browser remembers nothing. Expiry is entirely server-side.

items.q: Why does the design count clicks asynchronously through a queue instead of incrementing a counter during the redirect?

options.t: Queues make the counts more accurate
options.why: Opposite — the async path is slightly LESS accurate (lag, possible drops), and we accept that. The win is protecting the hot path, not precision.

options.t: Redis can't do increments
options.why: Redis increments happily (INCR). The issue is architectural: any synchronous side-work adds latency and a failure dependency to every single redirect.

options.t: Synchronous counting would add 12K writes/sec and a new failure dependency to the latency-critical path, for data that tolerates delay and small loss
options.why: Right. Click counts are decorative — seconds of lag is fine. Batched aggregation turns 12K events/sec into a few dozen DB writes/sec, and a dead queue degrades stats, never redirects.

options.t: It's cheaper to store counts in a queue
options.why: The queue isn't storage — it's a shock absorber. Counts still land in a stats table; they just arrive batched and off the critical path.

items.q: Peak traffic, 12K redirects/sec, and your entire Redis cache tier dies. In this chapter's design, what actually happens?

options.t: Redirects start failing until the cache is restored
options.why: Only if you built cache-required instead of cache-aside. The DB holds the full mapping; the cache is an accelerator, not the source of truth.

options.t: DynamoDB absorbs the full 12K/sec, p99 rises maybe 10ms, and users don't notice — because we sized the DB for this day
options.why: Yes. 12K key-value gets/sec is well within a properly provisioned Dynamo table. 'The design survives its cache dying' is a sentence you earn by sizing the fallback honestly.

options.t: You must immediately fail over to a standby region
options.why: A regional failover for a cache outage is using a crane to pick up a pencil. The DB fallback handles it in-region; multi-region is for region-scale failures.

options.t: The redirect service serves stale links from local memory only
options.why: A local hot-links cache helps with the top handful of keys, but it can't cover the long tail. The real absorber is the database — that's why the miss path was sized.

items.q: A teammate ships 301 redirects to cut server load. Three weeks later, marketing reports click counts are mysteriously low and still dropping. What happened?

options.t: Browsers cached the 301s, so repeat clicks go straight to the destination without touching your servers — invisible to counting, and worsening as more browsers cache more links
options.why: Exactly the failure mode. Each browser only shows you a link's FIRST click. The decay over weeks is the tell: caches are progressively filling. Revocation is broken the same way.

options.t: The queue consumer is lagging
options.why: Lag delays counts; it doesn't shrink them, and it doesn't correlate with a redirect-code deploy. The 'still dropping over weeks' shape points at accumulating browser caches.

options.t: Users click short links less over time naturally
options.why: Maybe marginally, but a step-change after a deploy plus steady decay is a system fingerprint, not a behavior trend. Correlate the metric drop with the 301 rollout.

options.t: DynamoDB TTL deleted active links
options.why: TTL only removes rows past their expires_at, which would cause 404 spikes, not silently shrinking counts on live links.

items.q: Overnight, your 404 rate jumps from 0.1% to 15% of requests, with traffic up 3x, spread across many IPs. Most likely explanation and first response?

options.t: Someone is scanning your keyspace for valid codes — enable negative caching, tighten per-IP rate limits, and check what your valid codes might expose
options.why: Random probes overwhelmingly miss (your links use 0.2% of the space), so scanners announce themselves as a 404 flood. This is exactly why 404 rate belongs on the dashboard as a security signal, not just an error metric.

options.t: The database lost rows — start a restore from backup
options.why: Data loss would spike 404s on PREVIOUSLY WORKING links, with normal traffic volume. 3x traffic of misses across many IPs is an attacker's fingerprint, not corruption's.

options.t: A deploy broke code parsing — roll back
options.why: Worth a 30-second check of the deploy timeline, but a parsing bug 404s legitimate existing links at normal volume. Tripled traffic that's mostly misses is enumeration.

options.t: Normal growth — provision more servers
options.why: Growth adds hits and misses proportionally; the 404 ratio stays flat. A ratio jumping 150x means the new traffic is almost all misses — nobody's real clicks look like that.

items.q: The counter table that leases ID blocks goes down for two hours at noon. What's the user-visible impact in this chapter's design?

options.t: Likely none: every server keeps minting from its already-leased block (hours of runway at 40 links/sec), and redirects never touch the counter at all
options.why: The payoff of leasing 1M-ID blocks: coordination happens a few times a day, so servers carry a long runway. Creation only stalls if the outage outlives everyone's blocks. Redirects are untouched by construction.

options.t: All link creation stops immediately
options.why: That's the raw-central-counter design failing. Leased blocks exist precisely so a counter outage burns runway, not availability.

options.t: Redirects fail because codes can't be decoded
options.why: Decoding a redirect never consults the counter — the code is looked up in the links table. The counter is write-path-only, and only at lease time.

options.t: Duplicate codes get minted while it's down
options.why: Blocks already leased are disjoint — servers can't collide with each other no matter how long the counter sleeps. Uniqueness is baked in at lease time.

items.q: With hash-based code generation, two different users shorten the same news article URL. What happens, and why is it a product bug?

options.t: The second user gets an error
options.why: No error — the write succeeds or is a no-op, which is what makes the bug silent. Both users walk away holding the same code.

options.t: Both get the same code, so they share one click counter and neither can expire or manage 'their' link independently
options.why: Deterministic hashing means same input, same code. Dedup sounds like a feature until per-user stats, per-user expiry, and takedown all break. Salting with user ID fixes it — and erases hashing's only advantage.

options.t: A collision retry gives the second user a different code automatically
options.why: The retry loop fires on collisions between DIFFERENT URLs. The same URL hashes identically every time — no collision is detected, that's the point of the bug.

options.t: Nothing — sharing codes is strictly good deduplication
options.why: Storage-wise, sure. Product-wise, two customers now co-own one analytics stream and one expiry setting. 'Whose link is it?' has no answer.

items.q: You enable DynamoDB TTL to clean up expired links and remove the expires_at check from the redirect path 'since TTL handles it.' What breaks?

options.t: Nothing — TTL is exactly for this
options.why: TTL is for cleanup, not correctness. Dynamo documents TTL deletion as best-effort, potentially lagging up to ~48 hours past expiry.

options.t: Expired links keep redirecting for up to ~48 hours, because TTL deletion is best-effort and lagged — the lazy check was the correctness mechanism
options.why: Right. A link that promised to die at midnight serves traffic well into tomorrow. Lazy check for correctness, TTL for hygiene — you need both, and only one is optional.

options.t: TTL deletes links early, causing 404s on live links
options.why: TTL never fires before the timestamp — the lag is always in the late direction. The bug window is 'expired but still served', not 'live but deleted'.

options.t: The cache serves the link forever regardless
options.why: There is a second, smaller bug here — cached entries need eviction on expiry — but the cache TTL (a day) bounds it. The 48-hour best-effort DB lag is the headline breakage.

items.q: One link goes on a viral tweet: 100K clicks/minute on a single code. Where does this design absorb it?

options.t: The permutation spreads the load across shards
options.why: The permutation randomizes which key it IS — but it's still one key. All 100K/min converge on one cache entry; hot keys can't be spread by hashing, only replicated or copied closer.

options.t: In caches: Redis serves the single hot key, and the redirect servers' small in-process LRU caps even that, since one immutable code→URL entry is trivially copyable everywhere
options.why: Right. 100K/min ≈ 1.7K/sec — Redis shrugs, and the local LRU means even a 100x hotter key just gets served from every app server's own memory. Immutable tiny values are the easiest hot-key case (chapter 2.6).

options.t: You must urgently reshard DynamoDB
options.why: The DB sees this key roughly once — the first miss — then the cache owns it. Resharding the durable store for a cache-layer phenomenon is solving the wrong tier.

options.t: Rate-limit clicks on that link to protect the system
options.why: Throttling legitimate users on your most successful link is the product harming itself. This load is tiny for a cache; absorb it, don't refuse it.

items.q: Interviewer: 'You picked DynamoDB. Wouldn't Postgres work?' The strongest reply:

options.t: "Honestly, yes — Postgres with the same cache in front handles 12K reads/sec fine. I chose Dynamo because the access pattern is a single key-value get, conditional writes handle the alias race, TTL handles expiry, and I don't operate failover myself. If the team already ran Postgres expertly, I'd flip."
options.why: Conceding what's true, re-anchoring on the actual reasons, and naming the condition that would flip the choice — that's how a committed decision survives pushback without turning into stubbornness.

options.t: "No — SQL can't handle this scale."
options.why: False, and the interviewer knows it: 12K/sec of primary-key lookups on 3 TB is comfortable Postgres territory. A defense built on a wrong claim collapses on the next question.

options.t: "Either works, whatever you prefer."
options.why: Retreating from your commitment at the first probe reads worse than never committing. The probe is an invitation to show your reasons, not a demand to surrender.

options.t: "Postgres would need heavy sharding for the 3 TB."
options.why: You did the math yourself: 3 TB fits one box. Contradicting your own estimation to defend a database choice is the fastest way to lose both points.

items.q: You're rolling out a new version of the permutation/encoder logic. Why does this deploy deserve more paranoia than a redirect-service deploy?

options.t: It's slower code
options.why: Performance isn't the fear — arithmetic is microseconds either way. The fear is correctness: bad codes, once minted and shared, are forever.

options.t: A bug here mints wrong or colliding codes into permanent public circulation — so it ships behind a flag with an offline verifier replaying IDs through old and new paths, asserting identical output
options.why: Right. A bad redirect deploy serves errors until rollback — recoverable. A bad encoder writes poison into the permanent dataset; links are out in the world and can't be recalled. Verify equivalence offline, canary at 1%.

options.t: The permutation is secret, so fewer engineers can review it
options.why: The constant is secret-ish; the code path is normally reviewable. The asymmetry is blast radius: encoder bugs are permanent, redirect bugs are transient.

options.t: It requires a coordinated database migration
options.why: No schema changes — same table, same columns. The danger is silent semantic drift in what gets written, which is exactly what a replay-and-compare verifier catches.

items.q: The interviewer asks you to commit to an ID-generation strategy. Which answer performs at the senior bar?

options.t: "Leased ranges plus a bijective permutation: servers lease 1M-ID blocks so coordination is rare, the shuffle makes codes non-sequential without collision risk. Weaknesses I'll own: the shuffle is obscurity not security, and crashed servers strand partial blocks — which costs 0.03% of a 3.5T space, so I don't care."
options.why: A commitment, the mechanism in one breath, and two self-identified weaknesses with one priced into irrelevance. Naming your design's flaws before the interviewer does is the strongest E5 signal in this entire problem.

options.t: "There are four options — counter, hashing, KGS, and ranges — each with trade-offs depending on requirements."
options.why: A correct taxonomy and zero judgment. The question was 'commit'; a survey answer to a commitment question is the exact hedge that caps candidates at mid-level.

options.t: "Snowflake IDs — that's what Twitter uses at massive scale."
options.why: Borrowed authority, poorly fitted: Snowflake's 64-bit timestamped IDs encode to ~11 base62 characters and embed a timestamp — long AND partially guessable, failing two of this problem's four constraints. Name-dropping without checking fit reads junior.

options.t: "A pre-generated key pool — it's the standard answer for this problem."
options.why: KGS genuinely works, but 'it's the standard answer' is the tell — justification by textbook, not by reasoning. Say WHY (pre-checked uniqueness, random codes) and address the cost (an extra service to babysit) and this becomes defensible.

items.q: Halfway through your walkthrough, the interviewer asks: 'What do you think is the actual hard part of this problem?' The crux-calibrated answer:

options.t: "Storing billions of URLs durably"
options.why: Your own estimation said 3 TB — one drive. Naming a solved problem as the crux tells the interviewer your numbers and your attention aren't connected.

options.t: "Generating billions of unique short codes across many servers with no central bottleneck and no guessable sequence"
options.why: That's the fire this question was invented to light. Every other component is routine plumbing; this one has four constraints in tension and a graveyard of plausible-but-flawed solutions.

options.t: "Handling the enormous redirect traffic"
options.why: 12K/sec of cacheable key-value reads is a well-trodden path — cache plus KV store, done. Calling routine load 'the hard part' inflates a solved problem.

options.t: "Designing the analytics pipeline"
options.why: Only because we scoped stats as 'lite'. Async queue plus batched increments is a pattern, not a puzzle. (Flip the requirement to billing-grade exact counts and this answer gets much more interesting.)

items.q: "What changes in your design at 10x traffic?" The senior answer for THIS system is:

options.t: "Almost nothing structural — more cache shards and a bigger Dynamo bill. 120K/sec is still cache-shaped, 30 TB is still small, the counter leases hourly instead of daily. What would force redesign isn't traffic, it's a requirement flip like exact-count billing."
options.why: The honest answer, with reasons, plus the insight that this design's pressure point is requirements, not scale. Resisting the urge to invent heroics for 10x is itself the senior signal — the design's shape was chosen so 10x is a bill.

options.t: "I'd move to a multi-region active-active architecture with consistent hashing across a fleet of cache tiers."
options.why: Multi-region is a fine LATENCY conversation, but as an answer to '10x traffic' it's unjustified machinery — 120K/sec doesn't need any of it. Reflexive escalation reads as not trusting your own numbers.

options.t: "I'd shard the database before anything else."
options.why: Sharding what? 30 TB of KV data in Dynamo is already automatically partitioned, and the permuted codes spread writes evenly. This answer ignores both the storage math and the DB choice already made.

options.t: "Everything — I'd redesign for 10x from scratch to be safe."
options.why: Throwing away a working design at the first stress question is the panic pattern. The interviewer wants to see you locate what actually bends — and here, honestly, almost nothing does.

items.q: A product manager wants to use your shortener for 'private' payslip links — security via the unguessable 7-character code, no login. Your call?

options.t: Refuse the premise: a short code is a public name, not an access control. The destination must authenticate. Cite the OneDrive/goo.gl scanning research — enumerated 'private' short links exposed documents at scale, and 7% of exposed accounts were writable
options.why: The 2016 'Gone in Six Characters' study is the closing argument: token spaces get scanned, and entropy only slows the scanner. Codes leak through referrer headers, chat previews, and logs anyway. Auth at the destination is non-negotiable for private data.

options.t: Agree — 3.5 trillion codes can't be brute-forced
options.why: 3.5T random probes is a lot, but your VALID codes cluster (0.2% density and growing), scanners run distributed for months, and codes also leak via referrers, previews, and logs. Microsoft and Google both retreated from exactly this bet.

options.t: Agree, but lengthen payslip codes to 12 characters
options.why: Longer tokens raise the scanning cost (this is what Google Maps did) but leave every leak channel open — referrer headers, link previews, shared screens. For payslips the answer is authentication, not a longer secret in the URL.

options.t: Agree, with per-IP rate limiting to block scanners
options.why: Rate limits are a speed bump for a botnet spreading probes across thousands of IPs over months. Defense that must win every day against a patient attacker isn't defense — it's a countdown.

items.q: Interviewer pushes: 'Your 302 choice means you pay to serve every repeat click forever. That's a big bill for vanity stats, no?' Best response:

options.t: "That bill IS the business — bit.ly survived losing Twitter's default slot precisely because the click log was sellable. But you're right that it's a real cost: if stats and revocation were ever descoped, I'd switch to 301 that day and let browsers absorb the repeats."
options.why: Ties the cost to the requirement it purchases, uses a true industry precedent, and names the exact condition that flips the decision. A committed choice plus its flip condition is judgment; a committed choice defended unconditionally is ego.

options.t: "Serving redirects is cheap, so the cost doesn't really matter."
options.why: Dodges instead of engaging. Cheap per-click times ten billion clicks a month is a real number; the senior move is owning the cost and showing what it buys, not waving it away.

options.t: "Good point — I'll switch to 301 to be safe."
options.why: Capitulating abandons the analytics and revocation requirements you committed to twenty minutes ago. Folding on a probe reads worse than the original choice ever could.

options.t: "I'd do 301 for free users and 302 for paying users."
options.why: Creative, but it quietly breaks abuse takedown: free-tier links — where the abuse lives — become browser-cached and irrevocable. A tiering idea that hands attackers the better tier fails the two-minute sniff test.

items.q: Closing minute. Which monitoring statement adds the most senior signal for this system?

options.t: "Four alerts: redirect p99, cache hit rate, queue lag — and 404 rate, which here is a security signal, not an error metric: a scanner enumerating the keyspace shows up as a 404 flood long before any other alarm."
options.why: Naming the metrics is table stakes; explaining why one of them means something unusual for THIS system — 404s as intrusion detection — shows the design and its threat model live in the same head.

options.t: "I'd monitor CPU, memory, and disk on all hosts."
options.why: Host metrics are the floor, and they say nothing about this system's promises. Monitoring should watch what you promised: latency, availability, and the abuse surface.

options.t: "I'd set up dashboards for all key metrics and review them weekly."
options.why: Process words with no content. WHICH metrics, and which ones page a human at 3am? The senior version commits to four numbers and can defend each.

options.t: "I'd alert on any error rate above zero to catch problems early."
options.why: A zero-tolerance alert on a public endpoint pages someone every time a user typos a link. Alert fatigue is how real incidents get slept through; thresholds exist to separate weather from fire.

items.q: The click-event queue is down and events are piling up in redirect-service memory. An engineer proposes blocking redirects until the queue recovers 'so we don't lose data.' Your ruling as the senior on call:

options.t: Ship the 302s, drop the events, emit an undercount metric
options.why: Correct — and note the correct answer is one line. Stats were scoped as approximate and lossy; redirects are the product. Trading the plane to save the passenger's snacks inverts the system's entire priority order. Bound the in-memory buffer, drop beyond it, count the drops.

options.t: Block redirects briefly — data loss is always worse than latency
options.why: 'Always' is doing junior work in that sentence. This data was DECLARED droppable at requirements time. Failing ten billion monthly redirects to protect approximate counters is the priority inversion the async design exists to prevent.

options.t: Buffer events to local disk with no size limit until the queue returns
options.why: Better instinct — degrade stats, not redirects — but 'no size limit' means a long outage fills the disk, and now the redirect host itself falls over. Unbounded buffers convert someone else's outage into yours.

options.t: Fail over click events to writing the database directly
options.why: The queue exists to protect the DB from 12K writes/sec; the fallback reintroduces exactly the load the design was built to avoid — during an incident, when you least want a second fire.
